title: Individual Contributions
introduction: This chapter documents each team member's independent investigation within assigned algorithm families.

sections.title: Muhammad Usama Fazal (TP086008): Ensemble Methods
sections.content_html: Investigated ensemble methods combining multiple base learners for improved robustness. Selected BaggingClassifier for highest baseline (90.37%) and explicit control over base estimators. Final model achieved 91.60% balanced accuracy (+1.36% improvement).

tables.caption: Ensemble Methods Baseline Comparison
tables.description: This baseline comparison evaluates three ensemble methods using default scikit-learn parameters. BaggingClassifier achieves the highest balanced accuracy (90.37%) and MCC (0.7997), outperforming RandomForestClassifier by 1.1 percentage points despite requiring significantly longer training time (20.75s vs 2.17s). ExtraTreesClassifier shows the weakest performance at 86.69% balanced accuracy, likely due to its extremely randomized splitting strategy being suboptimal for the structured NSL-KDD feature space. The MCC values confirm the balanced accuracy rankings, with BaggingClassifier's 0.7997 indicating strong correlation between predictions and actual labels across both classes.

tables.caption: Ensemble Hyperparameter Tuning
tables.description: Hyperparameter tuning reveals a non-monotonic relationship between ensemble size and performance. Increasing n_estimators from 100 to 150 yields a substantial 1.36% improvement in balanced accuracy, demonstrating that additional base learners enhance the ensemble's ability to capture diverse decision boundaries. However, further increasing to 200 estimators shows diminishing returns with only 0.98% improvement over baseline, suggesting the ensemble reaches diversity saturation. This pattern indicates that 150 estimators represents the optimal trade-off between computational cost and predictive performance for this dataset.

tables.caption: Top Features: BaggingClassifier
tables.description: Feature importance analysis reveals that content-based features dominate the BaggingClassifier's decision-making process. The src_bytes feature (source-to-destination byte count) emerges as the most discriminative with 18.7% importance, followed by dst_bytes (15.6%) representing return traffic volume. These two byte-count features together account for over one-third of total feature importance, indicating that traffic volume patterns are highly indicative of attack versus normal behavior. The count feature (connections to same host) ranks third at 9.8%, capturing temporal patterns that distinguish reconnaissance and flooding attacks from legitimate traffic.

tables.caption: Computational Performance: Ensemble
tables.description: The computational profile of BaggingClassifier reveals the characteristic ensemble trade-off between training cost and inference efficiency. Training requires 79.41 seconds to construct 150 decision tree base learners, each fitted on bootstrap samples of the training data. However, prediction time remains efficient at 0.89 seconds for the entire test set (22,544 samples), translating to approximately 0.04 milliseconds per sample—well within real-time IDS requirements. The 45.2 MB model size reflects storage of 150 complete decision trees, which may be a consideration for memory-constrained deployment environments but is manageable for modern systems.

sections.title: Md Sohel Rana (TP086217): Non-Linear Methods
sections.content_html: Investigated non-linear methods capable of capturing complex relationships. DecisionTreeClassifier selected for highest baseline (91.12%) and interpretability. Final model achieved 91.19% balanced accuracy (+0.07%).

tables.caption: Non-Linear Methods Baseline Comparison
tables.description: This baseline comparison reveals dramatic performance differences among non-linear methods. DecisionTreeClassifier achieves 91.12% balanced accuracy with the highest MCC (0.8147), demonstrating that recursive partitioning effectively captures the complex decision boundaries in network traffic data. KNeighborsClassifier shows moderate performance (85.82%) but suffers from computational overhead (4.90s) due to distance calculations across all training samples. GaussianNB performs poorly (61.72%) with an MCC of only 0.3343, indicating that the naive independence assumption between features is severely violated in network traffic data where features like byte counts and connection durations are inherently correlated.

tables.caption: Decision Tree Hyperparameter Tuning
tables.description: Depth constraint tuning demonstrates the delicate balance between model complexity and generalization. The unlimited-depth baseline achieves 91.12% balanced accuracy, while restricting to max_depth=15 causes a 0.59% performance decrease, indicating this constraint is too aggressive and prevents the tree from capturing necessary complexity. Setting max_depth=20 achieves the optimal result at 91.19%, providing a marginal 0.07% improvement over baseline while introducing regularization that prevents overfitting to noise in the training data. The narrow performance range (0.67% total variation) suggests the decision tree is robust to depth parameters within reasonable bounds.

tables.caption: Top Features: DecisionTreeClassifier
tables.description: The DecisionTreeClassifier's feature importance rankings align with the ensemble results but with higher concentration. The src_bytes feature dominates with 23.1% importance, higher than in the BaggingClassifier, reflecting the single tree's reliance on this highly discriminative feature for early splits. Together, the top three features (src_bytes, dst_bytes, count) account for 53.3% of total importance, compared to 44.1% in the ensemble. This concentration provides interpretability advantages for security analysts who can understand that abnormal byte transfer patterns and connection frequencies are primary attack indicators, enabling development of intuitive alert rules and manual verification procedures.

tables.caption: Computational Performance: Non-Linear
tables.description: The DecisionTreeClassifier exhibits exceptional computational efficiency across all metrics. Training completes in just 0.87 seconds—approximately 90 times faster than the BaggingClassifier's 79.41 seconds—while achieving comparable accuracy (91.19% vs 91.60%). Prediction requires only 0.02 seconds for the full test set, enabling processing of over 1 million samples per second. The O(log n) prediction complexity means each sample traverses a path proportional to tree depth rather than dataset size, ensuring scalability for high-throughput network monitoring scenarios. This efficiency makes the decision tree particularly attractive for resource-constrained or latency-sensitive deployment environments.

sections.title: Imran Shahadat Noble (TP087895): Support Vector Methods
sections.content_html: Investigated linear support vector methods. Consistent ~79% ceiling across both methods suggested fundamental linear separability limitation. Final model achieved 79.18% balanced accuracy (+0.11%).

tables.caption: Support Vector Methods Baseline Comparison
tables.description: The baseline comparison between LinearSVC and RidgeClassifier reveals remarkably similar performance despite different optimization objectives, strongly suggesting a fundamental linear separability limitation rather than algorithm deficiency. LinearSVC achieves 78.62% balanced accuracy through margin maximization, while RidgeClassifier achieves marginally better 79.10% using least-squares with L2 regularization. The small 0.48 percentage point difference and near-identical MCC values (0.5782 vs 0.5883) indicate both algorithms are constrained by the same ceiling—the inherent non-linear structure of network attack patterns that cannot be captured by a linear hyperplane in the 121-dimensional feature space.

tables.caption: Support Vector Hyperparameter Tuning
tables.description: Hyperparameter tuning confirms the linear model's fundamental capacity limitation through an exceptionally flat response surface. The entire parameter search space yields only 0.22% performance variation, from 79.10% to 79.18% balanced accuracy. Applying balanced class weights provides the largest improvement (+0.11%), addressing the slight class imbalance between normal and attack samples. Reducing regularization strength (alpha from 1.0 to 0.1) produces negligible change (+0.01%), indicating the model is not underfitting due to over-regularization but rather due to insufficient model complexity. This flat optimization landscape is a diagnostic signature of model capacity saturation.

tables.caption: Linear Model Characteristics
tables.description: The RidgeClassifier operates by learning 121 coefficients that define a linear hyperplane decision boundary in the feature space. The coefficient range of [-0.89, 0.94] indicates balanced feature contributions without extreme weights that might suggest numerical instability or overfitting to specific features. However, this linear decision boundary fundamentally limits the model's expressiveness—it can only separate classes that are linearly separable in the original feature space. Network attacks often exhibit complex, non-linear patterns where the combination of feature values (not just their weighted sum) determines attack likelihood, explaining the 12+ percentage point accuracy gap compared to non-linear methods.

tables.caption: Computational Performance: Linear
tables.description: The RidgeClassifier achieves the fastest computational performance across all metrics, representing the efficiency advantage of linear models. Training completes in 0.50 seconds through closed-form matrix inversion, bypassing iterative optimization required by more complex models. Prediction requires only 0.01 seconds for 22,544 test samples—a simple matrix multiplication operation enabling processing of over 2 million samples per second. The 0.1 MB model size (storing only 121 coefficients plus bias) is 450 times smaller than the BaggingClassifier, enabling deployment on severely resource-constrained edge devices. However, this computational efficiency comes at a significant accuracy cost of 12+ percentage points compared to non-linear alternatives.

sections.title: Cross-Student Synthesis
sections.content_html:
Key Findings:

  • Non-Linear Essential: 91%+ balanced accuracy vs. 79% for linear methods
  • Optimization Impact: Ensemble +1.36%, DecisionTree +0.07%, Ridge +0.11%
  • Error Profiles: Ensemble optimal balance; DecisionTree lowest bias; Ridge high irreducible bias
